extracted.intended_audience: USPTO personnel, patent examiners, patent practitioners, policymakers, and other stakeholders engaged in US patent eligibility assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for evaluating whether claimed inventions satisfy U.S. patent subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101, including application of the Supreme Court’s Alice/Mayo two-step framework and USPTO-specific procedures (steps 1, 2A, 2B) across technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1 of the USPTO analysis addresses whether the claimed invention falls into one of the four categories recited in 35 U.S.C. §101 (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). This is the threshold inquiry and distinct from other patentability requirements (utility, novelty, non-obviousness, written description, enablement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain implicit limits on eligibility exist: abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena are not patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has long recognized these judicial exceptions. Examiners must identify whether a claim implicates any of these exceptions when performing eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO implements this framework within its own procedures (see steps 2A and 2B). Under step two the court’s search for an 'inventive concept' helps decide whether the claim transforms an ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO unified eligibility analysis (Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO combines criteria into a single analysis: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (determine if claim is directed to a judicial exception and second prong whether it integrates the exception into a practical application), Step 2B (determine whether additional elements amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners use step 2A to evaluate 'directed to' and, if a judicial exception is present, proceed to step 2B to evaluate whether additional elements provide an inventive concept. If a claim is found eligible at any point, the eligibility analysis stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — first prong: determine whether claim recites a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim limitations recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon by analyzing the claim limitations in connection with scientific principles, natural laws, or known categories of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For laws of nature or natural phenomena, evaluate limitations in connection with scientific principles (e.g., laws of thermodynamics, Newton's laws). For products of nature, determine whether a nature-based product has characteristics markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart (Myriad considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — second prong: integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application (in which case the claim is eligible) rather than being directed to the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include whether additional claim elements improve the functioning of a computer or other technology, whether the claim merely applies the exception in a particular environment or field of use, or whether a claim step applies or uses the exception to effect a specific treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition. If the claim passes this prong, the eligibility analysis stops and the claim is eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of abstract ideas by groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are identified by whether a claim limitation falls into one or more groupings derived from judicial precedent: mathematical concepts, mental processes, and certain methods of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO revised its approach (January 2019) to require examiners to identify abstract ideas by these groupings (rather than attempting to compare each claim to every court-identified abstract idea) to promote consistency and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature / 'markedly different' characteristics test (Myriad)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a nature-based product (product of nature) is evaluated to determine whether it has 'markedly different characteristics' from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics (e.g., Myriad's isolated DNA claims lacked such characteristics), the claim may be directed to a product of nature and thus be a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' / inventive concept analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., supply an inventive concept sufficient to render the claim patent eligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO personnel use similar considerations as in step 2A. If additional elements are merely conventional or generic, they typically do not supply the needed inventive concept and the claim can be rejected for lack of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional consideration (evidence requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that an additional element is 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' to a skilled artisan in the relevant field, that conclusion is a factual determination requiring written support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner relies on the 'well-understood, routine, conventional' rationale in step 2B, the examiner must provide a written factual determination (with citation/support) that the element or combination is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry (per USPTO memoranda and MPEP guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction principle — broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole when performing eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO flowchart and guidance instruct examiners to interpret claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language as part of determining eligibility and whether amendments could place the claim within a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment pathway and procedural handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is not eligible as written, consider whether the claim can be amended to fall within a statutory category or otherwise be framed to integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner makes an eligibility rejection, the applicant is given an opportunity to respond (e.g., amend the claim or argue why the claim is eligible). The examiner will also evaluate other patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, written description, enablement) regardless of the eligibility determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of 'improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology'
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that 'improves the functioning of a computer or any other technology or technical field' is a relevant consideration that may indicate the claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration has been applied in multiple decisions and USPTO memoranda; if a claim limitation meaningfully improves computer functionality or another technical field, it supports eligibility under the second prong of step 2A or in step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples, training, and supplemental materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO provides numerous examples (46 examples covering AI, biotechnology, business methods, diagnostics, pharmaceuticals, precision medicine, software, etc.) and training to promote consistent application of eligibility guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and stakeholders should consult these examples and training resources (posted on the USPTO subject matter eligibility webpage) to understand how the guidance applies to various fact patterns and technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural stop/start rules in eligibility flow (stop analysis when eligible)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is determined not to recite a judicial exception or is found to integrate the exception into a practical application (passes step 2A prong two), the eligibility analysis stops and the claim is eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when a claim is directed to a judicial exception and fails the practical application prong does the examination proceed to step 2B. This procedural flow is reflected in the USPTO flowchart in MPEP §2106 and accompanying guidance.
